6. The case against

Dominant risk (financial): RELX's per-share compounding may mask fading operating leverage through a £2.25bn buyback funded while leverage is rising.

Earliest observable: The 22 October 2026 trading update will say whether strong underlying growth and cost growth below revenue still hold; the FY2026 results, checked by 15 February 2027, will print cash conversion and net debt/EBITDA against P3's hard thresholds (financial calendar, half-year results).

Net debt rose to £8.733bn from £7.443bn a year earlier while £1.75bn was spent on buybacks in six months. Reported operating profit still grew, but the valuation case should not silently capitalize management's adjusted growth if future repurchases require leverage or cash conversion slips.

The high margin also invites competition. Thomson Reuters says CoCounsel reached one million professional users in February 2026; RELX must keep turning its content into paid workflows rather than let a rival or a general model capture the interface (competitor adoption disclosure).

Combined exposure: REL.L is not in the human book, so the existing name weight is 0%; the buy adds to Europe, currently 6.43% of the human book, rather than to its already dominant US exposure (signals.json).

Why this is not the 7532.T mistake again: this is not a rebound story. The case starts with four filed years of GAAP margin and capital productivity, checks the latest half-year operating and cash evidence, uses valuation only as a gate, and makes buyback-supported per-share growth the subject of both falsifier tiers.

The share may be cheap because earnings are already rolling over. Utility customers have excess inventory and installation bottlenecks, while the higher power-transformer mix takes longer to produce; backlog can therefore look reassuring for years before becoming cash, and factory delays would hurt both revenue and margins (H1 update).

The strongest reason not to buy is that the market may correctly see peak transformer margins, acquisition- flattered growth and an expensive capacity build meeting normalized utility demand. The 12.70× multiple is only the gate RSGN.SW passed; it does not make that cycle risk disappear.

Do not buy this if you want a predictable compounder. 1. Where the world is

What is true

The world is absorbing a genuine increase in electricity use, not just an AI-market narrative. The IEA expects global electricity demand to grow 3.6% in 2026 and 3.8% in 2027, versus 3.0% in 2025; it also expects renewables to overtake coal generation in 2026 and says grid expansion and modernisation are critical to integrating that supply (IEA mid-year update). The local data agree that the physical inputs have moved: copper is up 46.95% over one year, while WTI is up 30.35% over one year but down 9.46% over three months (local macro data).

That investment boom sits beside a less comfortable macro picture. The IMF forecasts 3.0% global growth in 2026 and says disinflation has stalled, with technology momentum offsetting the drag from war (IMF July update). Markets show the same split: Nasdaq is up 23.06% over one year and the S&P 500 19.37%, while the Hang Seng is down 0.13%; US five- and ten-year yields are up 21.14% and 11.66% respectively over one year (local macro data).

Paper performance

Generated 2026-09-24 23:02 by npm run pot-report, from history.json closes.

Every name this pot has named, marked from the day it was named, as if bought at that day's close and held. Nothing has been bought — pot cash is £0 and no contribution has been made, so this is not P&L. It exists because positions.js scores nothing until money is committed, which leaves the phase where you are deciding whether to commit with no measure at all.

Every row below is noise. Not one of the 146 marks has reached 20 trading days — the oldest is 19. Read this page for whether the plumbing works, not for whether the picks are any good.

Returns are in each name's local currency. FX is excluded on purpose: the question here is whether the name was a good call, not what a sterling investor would have banked. That second question matters — 7532.T sits in strategy.md as a yen-depreciation regret — and earns its own column when real money makes it a real return.

Deep dive proposals

Each proposal is marked separately, including re-proposals of a name already proposed: a name that keeps clearing the bar at a different price is making a different call each time, and averaging them would hide exactly that. ×N means the same name cleared the bar N times on one day — the cycle runs several times daily and those share a single closing price, so they are one mark and N calls, not N marks.

Run ledger

Generated 2026-09-24 23:02 by npm run pot-report, from the Codex session transcripts under ~/.codex/sessions/ — never from what an agent said about itself.

Cost

Cash cost: £0. Codex is authenticated against a ChatGPT subscription (codex login status → "Logged in using ChatGPT"), so nothing is billed per token. What a run spends is subscription allowance and wall-clock time.

The token columns are kept because that is D12's whole purpose: if this ever moves to metered API credits these are the numbers that would be charged, and runs either side of the switch stay comparable. Fresh is input not served from cache — the part a metered call charges full rate for.
